general:
About

This website accompanies a research project at TU Berlin and UdK Berlin about children's scribbles. The project asks what these marks are, if you set aside the question of what they represent or what they reveal about the child who made them.

Since the late nineteenth century, researchers and clinicians have tended to interpret children's drawings either as stages on the way to figurative representation, or as diagnostic material. The artist Mike Kelley demonstrated how readily this interpretive tendency becomes projection in his 1995 work We Communicate Only Through Our Shared Dismissal of the Pre-linguistic, in which he wrote invented psychiatric captions for children's drawings, showing how easily adults impose pathology and hierarchy onto marks that simply have their own logic [1].

The American researcher Rhoda Kellogg spent decades collecting over a million children's drawings from around the world and found that the same basic forms keep appearing everywhere, in the same developmental order, regardless of culture [2]. The Swiss researchers Dieter Maurer and Claudia Riboni, working at the Zürcher Hochschule der Künste, extended this research over several decades and proposed that formal, non-representational graphic organisation always precedes any attempt at depiction [3]. The child does not begin by trying to draw things. The child begins with form.

The central hypothesis of this research is that those early, non-referential forms may share structural properties with what cognitive scientists call image schemata: pre-linguistic patterns of embodied experience, such as containment, path, balance, and force, that organise perception and thought before and below the level of language [4][5]. If this is the case, children's scribbles might offer a way to study, visualise, and enact these cognitive structures in material and temporal form. The website explores this hypothesis through four tools: a visual taxonomy, an annotation system, a drawing studio, and an association map.
taxonomy:
Kellogg's original classification covers many more categories than the ones presented here. Her full taxonomy includes figurative groups such as Humans, Animals, Buildings, Vegetation, and Transportation. This research focuses exclusively on the non-referential portion of the taxonomy, from Basic Scribbles through Placement Patterns, Emergent Diagram Shapes, Diagrams, Combines, Aggregates, Mandalas, Suns, and Radials.

This choice is not arbitrary. It follows the central finding of Maurer and Riboni's research: that abstract, purely formal graphic phenomena appear and develop autonomously, before any figurative or analogical relation to objects emerges [3]. The categories selected here are those in which marks do not yet point to anything outside themselves. They are not failed attempts at depiction. They are, as Maurer and Riboni argue, a primary and independent domain of graphic organisation that precedes representation and cannot be reduced to it. For this reason, the figurative categories of Kellogg's taxonomy fall outside the scope of this project.

There is a further reason this reconstruction exists. Kellogg's original taxonomy is accessible only through her printed books, which are out of print and expensive, or through scans available on the Internet Archive. The Internet Archive is, at the time of writing, under sustained legal and political pressure from large commercial interests seeking to restrict free access to digitised knowledge, pressure that reflects a broader effort by corporations and governments to enclose, commodify, and control the cultural commons. The scans that do exist are also of limited quality. To our knowledge, no complete, clean, and openly accessible visual reference for the non-referential portion of Kellogg's taxonomy currently exists.

Beyond accessibility, there is a methodological reason to redo this work from scratch. The illustrations in Kellogg's books are static diagrams. The drawings in this taxonomy are not. Each one was produced on a digital tablet and saved as a full spatiotemporal recording: every point drawn, in sequence, with its timestamp and pressure value, in addition to a static image and an animated version. This means each illustration is also a record of how it was made, preserving the gesture, the timing, and the movement that produced it. This is relevant to understanding the procedural logic that Maurer and Riboni identify as fundamental to early graphic development [3], and it is potentially useful as training material for computational models intended to recognise and classify these forms.
annotator:
The Kellogg archive available at early-pictures.ch [6] is an invaluable research resource: thousands of scanned children's drawings, carefully organised and made freely accessible by the research group of Dieter Maurer and Claudia Riboni. The archive was designed as an empirical and pedagogical tool for human researchers, and it works well for that purpose.

For the purposes of building a computational dataset, however, it presents a structural limitation that has nothing to do with the quality of the archive itself. Each drawing is assigned a single primary category. Most drawings, however, contain elements from several levels of the taxonomy simultaneously. A drawing classified as a Sun will also contain a closed circle, placement pattern elements, and possibly radial lines and other sub-structures. A single label does not capture this layered composition.

The annotator is a tool developed to address this. It allows drawings from the archive to be assigned multiple simultaneous labels, distinguishing between the spatial organisation of the drawing on the page, its primary graphic configuration, and any additional co-present elements. Every change is logged with a full audit trail. Visitors to this website can browse the annotations in read-only mode.
is_studio:
Image schemata are a concept introduced simultaneously and independently by Mark Johnson in The Body in the Mind (1987) [4] and George Lakoff in Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987) [5]. The theory proposes that a significant part of human conceptual structure, including abstract reasoning, is grounded in recurring patterns of sensorimotor experience. These patterns, which Johnson and Lakoff call image schemata, emerge from the body's repeated interactions with the physical world: the experience of being inside or outside something gives rise to the CONTAINER schema; the experience of moving from one place to another gives rise to the PATH schema; the experience of maintaining equilibrium gives rise to the BALANCE schema; the experience of exerting or resisting force gives rise to a family of force schemata including COMPULSION, BLOCKAGE, COUNTERFORCE, and ENABLEMENT. The theory has remained central to cognitive linguistics and embodied cognition research, and has been developed and refined by subsequent researchers including Hampe and Grady [7], Mandler [7], and Zlatev [7], among others.

One recurring difficulty in this field is the visual representation of image schemata. Because they are dynamic structures that unfold in time and involve change, force, and spatial relation, static diagrams can only partially capture them. The diagrams used across the cognitive linguistics literature have no shared formal language and are not mutually comparable. The Diagrammatic Image Schema Language (DISL), developed by Hedblom, Neuhaus, and Mossakowski (2025) [8], represents the most systematic attempt so far to address this: a standardised notation in which each schema is decomposed into conceptual primitives and described as a sequence of spatial scenes. DISL is itself a static notation in the sense that it produces a strip of discrete frames, but it is formally defined and internally consistent in a way that previous informal diagrams were not, and it can in principle be serialised and processed computationally. A related research direction by Olivier and Bouraoui (2025) [9] argues that any adequate formalism for image schemata must be qualitative, typed, temporal, and capable of non-monotonic reasoning, since image schemata involve default behaviours, force dynamics, and change over time.

The IS Studio is a speculative tool based on the hypothesis at the centre of this research: that children's scribbles, when recorded as full spatiotemporal sequences, might offer a way to enact and explore image schemata in material form. The association map proposes structural correspondences between Kellogg graphic categories and image schemata. A spiral, for example, shares structural features with PATH, CYCLE, and COMPULSION. A closed circle shares structural features with CONTAINER. A radial pattern shares structural features with CENTER-PERIPHERY and BALANCE. Whether these correspondences are meaningful in a deeper cognitive sense is an open question this research does not claim to resolve. The studio offers a way to explore them in practice.
map:
The association map connects the visual taxonomy reconstructed in this project, covering the non-referential portion of Kellogg's classification, to an inventory of image schemata. It is presented as an interactive network graph. Each node represents either a Kellogg graphic category or an image schema. Edges connect them according to proposed structural correspondences, weighted to distinguish primary from secondary associations.

The map is speculative. It is not derived from empirical data about what children think or intend when they draw, which is not directly accessible. It is derived from the structural properties of the graphic forms themselves, read against the definitions of image schemata in the cognitive linguistics literature. A closed circle produces an inside and an outside: this corresponds structurally to the CONTAINER schema. A cross connects two axes at a point: this corresponds structurally to LINK and CONTACT. The map proposes that these correspondences are consistent enough to be worth making explicit, and uses them as the basis for the drawing instructions in the IS Studio. It is a working document and will be revised as the annotation dataset grows and as IS Studio sessions accumulate.
cv:
The 3866 segmented scribbles in this archive are subjected here to a computer vision pipeline that produces, for each drawing, a set of complementary visualisations. Three families of readings are computed, each grounded in a different procedural commitment.

The first family is geometric. A sequence of deterministic algorithms decomposes each scribble into structural components: a continuous density field obtained as the gradient magnitude of a smoothed binary segmentation, a one-pixel skeleton extracted via morphological thinning, and the notable points along the skeleton where lines terminate (endpoints, with a single skeleton neighbour) or intersect (junctions, with three or more). These readings are purely formal. They follow fixed rules from classical image analysis and make no claim regarding what the drawing represents.

The second family is neural. DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023), a vision transformer pretrained by Meta AI on a corpus of 142 million unsupervised images, is applied to each scribble in zero-shot inference, with frozen weights. No fine-tuning on the archive is performed. For each drawing the model produces a set of attention maps, distributing weight from the classification token toward the image patches across twelve parallel heads. The heads, which during pretraining have developed distinct specialisations, yield divergent readings of the same mark: some emphasise edges and transitions, others coherent regions, others spatial relations across the image. The model has not been told what a scribble is, and the vast majority of its training corpus consists of natural photographs. It nevertheless responds to every drawing in the archive, identifying regions of structural coherence whose alignment with the visible mark varies from drawing to drawing and from head to head.

The third family is the fusion of the previous ones. The geometric and neural readings do not always converge, and their divergence is itself informative. Derived maps make the agreements and dissonances explicit: a geometric mean of attention and density isolates regions where both perspectives concur on the presence of structure; an absolute difference exposes where they diverge. In parallel, a high-dimensional feature vector concatenates the neural representation (768 values from the classification token) with the geometric measurements (seven normalised metrics), producing a single 775-dimensional descriptor per drawing, weighted at 70% neural and 30% geometric. This descriptor supports similarity search across the archive and provides a foundation for future supervised learning.

The pipeline described here constitutes a preparatory layer. Its outputs (geometric features, neural readings, fused vectors, projections) are not endpoints in themselves but components of a larger trajectory. Read together with the annotations being collected through the Annotator and with the image schema correspondences elaborated in the IS Studio, they are intended to support the eventual training of a visual classifier specialised on the Kellogg/Maurer archive: a model capable of analysing a scribble, or in principle any image with comparable graphic properties, and identifying within it the Kellogg categories and associated image schemata that structure it. The present readings are the substrate on which such a classifier could be built. The annotations are its supervisory signal. The image schema framework is its interpretive horizon.

Three views organise these readings. Single Image displays one scribble at a time, cycling continuously through its twenty-two visualisations as a slow respiration. Archive Map projects the entire dataset into two dimensions via UMAP, producing a cartography of the archive in which proximate drawings are formally similar according to the chosen lens. Comparative Grid allows the dataset to be filtered and sorted by the quantitative metrics drawn from the geometric pipeline.
cv_single:
Single Image

A single drawing is shown, cycling continuously through the twenty-two visualisations available for it. 

The first image is the original mark, isolated from its sheet.

The next four are produced by deterministic procedures applied to the binary segmentation: a continuous density field, a one-pixel skeleton, the set of stroke endpoints, and the set of junctions (none of these readings involves learning: they are computed by fixed algorithms drawn from classical image analysis).

The following fifteen are derived from DINOv2, a vision transformer pretrained on a corpus of 142 million images. The model has not been fine-tuned on this archive: it is applied in zero-shot inference, with frozen weights. What is shown for each scribble is a set of attention maps. 

A vision transformer divides each input image into a regular grid of small patches; in this configuration, a 280-pixel image is divided into 400 patches of 14 by 14 pixels. The model processes these patches through twelve successive blocks. Within each block, every patch attends to every other patch through a mechanism that distributes weight according to twelve parallel heads, each of which has developed during pretraining a distinct specialisation: some heads emphasise edges and local contrast, others coherent regions, others long-range spatial relations.

Alongside the patches, the model maintains a single additional token, the classification token, which aggregates information from the entire image. The maps shown here visualise the attention weights flowing from this classification token to the image patches in the final block of the network. Each head produces its own such map, exposing where in the image that head is concentrating. The maps are shown one head at a time, alongside an average across all heads. The model has not been told what a scribble is, and there is no reason to expect its heads to behave consistently across the archive. Some readings track the visible mark closely; others fall on regions of paper where no mark is present, or distribute attention diffusely across the entire image. Both outcomes are part of the experimental record of applying a model trained on natural photographs to graphic traces that precede the depiction of objects.

The final two images are fusions. The first is a geometric mean of the neural attention and the deterministic field, isolating regions where both readings indicate the presence of structure. The second is the absolute difference between them, where the two perspectives disagree.

A control panel allows the breathing to be paused, a different drawing to be loaded, or specific readings to be excluded from the cycle. Below the image, a row of ten thumbnails shows the nearest neighbours of the current drawing in the fused feature space described under Archive Map.
cv_map:
Archive Map

This view displays all 3866 drawings of the archive simultaneously, as points on a plane. The position of each point is determined by the formal properties of the corresponding drawing: scribbles whose readings are similar are placed near each other; scribbles whose readings differ are placed apart. The map is not a layout in any geographical or representational sense. It is a projection of the archive into two dimensions according to a chosen criterion of resemblance.

The criterion is constructed as follows. For each drawing, two vectors are derived. The first contains seven measurements produced by the deterministic pipeline, including ink density, skeleton length per ink unit, junction count, number of connected components, and a composite complexity score, each normalised against the distribution of values across the archive. The second contains 768 values produced by DINOv2 as the output of its classification token, that is, the model's compressed internal representation of the entire image. The two are concatenated, the neural component weighted at 70% and the geometric at 30%, yielding a single vector of 775 values per drawing. These vectors are not interpretable individually, but distances between them encode an aggregated notion of similarity that combines visual and structural criteria.

To produce the map, these high-dimensional vectors are passed through UMAP, a dimensionality reduction algorithm that constructs a graph of local neighbourhood relations in the original space and seeks a two-dimensional layout in which the graph structure is preserved as faithfully as possible. The result preserves clusters and local proximities reliably; global distances are distorted in a controlled fashion, prioritising local over global structure.

Three lenses are available. The default uses the fused vector. A second uses only the neural component, showing the organisation of the archive when restricted to the model's internal representation. A third uses only the geometric component, showing the structure that emerges from quantitative measurements alone. Differences between the three layouts indicate where the neural and geometric readings converge or diverge in their organisation of the archive.

Points may be coloured by Kellogg primary category, by complexity score, or left uncoloured. The first colouring exposes the relation between the Kellogg taxonomy and the formal organisation produced by the system: where Kellogg classes coincide with visible clusters in the projection, the categories track properties also detectable by the pipeline; where they do not, the categories track something else.

Hovering on a point shows a thumbnail and identifier. Clicking opens the drawing in Single Image. The map can be panned and zoomed.
cv_grid:
Comparative Grid

This view presents the archive as a filterable grid of thumbnails ordered by the deterministic metrics. Where the Archive Map projects similarity in aggregate, the Comparative Grid isolates individual quantitative axes and allows the dataset to be interrogated along them.

The metrics are those computed by the geometric pipeline: ink ratio (proportion of pixels covered by mark), skeleton ratio (length of the topological skeleton divided by image area), junction count (number of intersection points), endpoint count (number of stroke terminations), connected component count (degree of fragmentation), and complexity score (a derived measure combining several of the above). Each is available as a range filter, with bounds set to the 5th and 95th percentiles of the archive distribution to exclude outliers from the slider extents. Multiple filters apply simultaneously. A category filter restricts the visible set to specified Kellogg classes.

A sort selector reorders the visible set by any of the metrics, ascending or descending. A display selector switches the visualisation rendered as thumbnail: original mark, geometric field, skeleton, neural attention, or fusion consensus. The chosen display applies to the entire visible set, so that the filtered archive can be inspected through a single chosen reading at once.

Hovering on a thumbnail shows the identifier and Kellogg label. Clicking opens the drawing in Single Image. The grid is rendered with viewport-windowed virtualisation: only the thumbnails currently visible are loaded.
